questions.prompt: What is "Capstone II" in this path, as defined in Lesson 1?
options: A marketing name for Solstice Appliance Group's internal IT department
The programmatic-development capstone that follows the declarative Capstone I, requiring Apex, triggers, tests, LWC, and an integration
A Salesforce certification exam
A sandbox type used only for integration testing
questions.explain: Capstone II is this course: the programmatic-development milestone that follows the declarative-only Capstone I, requiring custom code (Apex, triggers, tests, LWC, REST integration) on top of a declarative baseline.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C (a certification exam) is wrong because Capstone II is a hands-on course project, not an exam; Salesforce certifications are a separate, unrelated credentialing track mentioned nowhere in this lesson's description of the capstone itself.

questions.prompt: Solstice's platform team is deciding how to automate approving a discount on an Opportunity when a manager's input is needed only occasionally and the approval criteria might change every few months as pricing policy shifts. Per Lesson 2's declarative-first principle, what's the right default choice?
options: Write a new Apex trigger on Opportunity, since triggers are always more powerful
Build it declaratively (Flow or an approval process), since the logic is likely to change for business reasons and an admin should be able to adjust it without a code deployment
Avoid automating it at all and handle every discount manually forever
Build it as a Lightning Web Component, since UI components handle all business logic
questions.explain: Lesson 2's rule is to default to declarative tools when the logic is likely to change for business reasons and an admin should be able to adjust it directly -- exactly the case here, as opposed to the warranty-claim validation reserved for Apex because of bulk-safety and testability needs.

questions.prompt: Match each object from Lesson 3's data model to what it represents.
right: An extended service plan a customer bought, determining coverage and a claimable dollar limit
The specific product a customer owns, connecting the sales side to the service side
A claim filed with the manufacturer when a repair is covered under warranty
One scheduled installation or repair visit tied to a Case, an Asset, and a Technician
questions.explain: Asset is the standard object tracking what a customer owns and the link between sales and service; Installation_Job__c is a scheduled visit; Warranty_Claim__c is a manufacturer claim; Service_Contract__c is the extended plan setting the coverage limit a claim is checked against.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lesson 4's security model for this platform.
options: Case's organization-wide default is Private, with broader visibility granted through role hierarchy and sharing rules rather than the OWD itself
Installation_Job__c uses Controlled by Parent (Case) as its OWD
A criteria-based sharing rule shares Opportunities where Stage = Closed Won as Read Only with the Service Agent role
Every object in this security model uses Public Read/Write as its OWD for simplicity
Warranty_Claim_Submitter access is granted directly on the Service Agent profile rather than through a permission set
questions.explain: Case is Private with visibility opened via role hierarchy/sharing rules; Installation_Job__c is Controlled by Parent; and the Closed Won sharing rule is real. Nothing in this model uses blanket Public Read/Write, and Warranty_Claim_Submitter access lives in a permission set, not directly on the profile, specifically because permission sets stack and are easier to assign selectively.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the JSON file that specifies which Salesforce edition and features a freshly created scratch org should have is called the scratch org ________ file.
questions.explain: The scratch org definition file (config/project-scratch-def.json) specifies the edition, license types, and preferences so every scratch org created from it is identically configured.

questions.prompt: Put these five Chapter 1 design activities in the order this capstone performs them.
questions.explain: Chapter 1 runs requirements first, then the architecture layers and governing principles, then the data model those layers depend on, then the security model built on top of that data model, and finally the environment/version-control setup needed before any building starts in Chapter 2 -- design fully precedes building, on purpose.

questions.prompt: What does the `with sharing` keyword do on an Apex class, per Lesson 7?
options: It enforces the running user's sharing rules and record-level access when the class queries data
It automatically writes test coverage for the class
It disables all governor limits for that class
It converts the class into a Lightning Web Component
questions.explain: with sharing enforces the running user's sharing rules and record-level access; without sharing is the opposite, letting a class see records the running user otherwise couldn't.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C (disabling governor limits) is a common misconception -- with sharing has nothing to do with resource limits like SOQL query or DML caps; it strictly controls record-level visibility during queries, and governor limits apply regardless of the sharing keyword used.

questions.prompt: A reviewer notices `WarrantyClaimTrigger` contains if/else logic deciding how to validate a claim, rather than just routing to a handler class. Per Lesson 9's pattern, what's the correct fix?
options: Leave it as is; triggers are expected to contain validation logic directly
Move all the real logic into a handler class, leaving the trigger itself only detecting context (before/after, insert/update) and calling the appropriate handler method
Delete the trigger entirely and replace it with a Flow
Add a second trigger on the same object to split the logic across two files
questions.explain: The one-trigger-per-object pattern keeps the trigger body thin -- detecting context and routing -- while all real logic lives in a separate, testable handler class, which is both easier to read and easier to unit test than logic embedded in the trigger file itself.

questions.prompt: Given `SELECT Id, (SELECT Id, Status__c FROM Installation_Jobs__r) FROM Case`, what kind of SOQL relationship query is this, per Lesson 8?
options: A child-to-parent query using dot notation
A parent-to-child subquery, using the child relationship name
A SOSL full-text search
An aggregate query using GROUP BY
questions.explain: This is a parent-to-child subquery: starting from Case (the parent) and pulling related Installation_Job__c records using the child relationship name Installation_Jobs__r, as opposed to dot notation which would walk the other direction, child to parent.

questions.prompt: Match each Flow Builder element from Lesson 6's Case to Installation Job Flow to its role.
right: Branches scheduling logic based on the Case's priority
Looks up whether an active Service_Contract__c exists for the Case's Asset
Calls the reusable Assign Technician logic
Runs when Create Records fails, creating a Case Comment instead of failing silently
questions.explain: Each element plays a distinct role in the complex Flow: Decision branches on priority, Get Records checks contract coverage, the subflow handles reusable technician assignment, and the fault path makes a Create Records failure visible instead of silent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 7, Apex allows a maximum of ________ SOQL queries in a single synchronous transaction.
questions.explain: The current Apex Developer Guide sets the synchronous SOQL query limit at 100 per transaction (200 in an asynchronous transaction).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about asynchronous Apex, per Lesson 11.
options: A future method can accept only primitive parameter types, not sObjects or custom objects
A Queueable class must implement Database.AllowsCallouts to be permitted to make an HTTP callout
Batch Apex's execute() method processes a default scope of 200 records per transaction unless a different scope size is specified
Future methods, Queueable jobs, Batch Apex, and Scheduled Apex each have completely separate daily limits with no shared ceiling
A future method can directly call another future method
questions.explain: Future methods only take primitives, Queueable callouts require Database.AllowsCallouts, and Batch Apex defaults to a 200-record scope. All four async types actually share one 24-hour rolling org limit rather than having fully separate ceilings, and future methods cannot chain-call other future methods.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9's order of execution, put these save-process steps in the correct order.
items: System and custom validation rules run
The database save happens (not yet committed)
questions.explain: A Salesforce save runs before-triggers first, then validation rules, then duplicate rules, then the (still uncommitted) database write, then after-triggers -- the order WarrantyClaimTrigger's beforeInsert relies on when it uses addError() instead of assuming a validation rule will catch an issue first.

questions.prompt: Why is `recordId` decorated with `@api` on the `technicianJobBoard` component, per Lesson 12?
options: Because @api makes the property load faster than a plain property
Because the platform itself sets recordId automatically when the component is placed on a record page, which requires the property to be public
Because @api is required on every property in every LWC with no exceptions
Because recordId must be tracked for in-place mutation
questions.explain: @api marks a property as public/settable from outside the component -- exactly what's needed since the platform (or a parent component) sets recordId automatically when the component sits on a record page.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, why must `updateJobStatus` be called imperatively from JavaScript rather than through `@wire`?
options: Because it should only run as the direct result of a user clicking a button, at a moment the component's own code controls, and it performs DML so it can't be cacheable
Because @wire cannot call any Apex method under any circumstances
Because imperative calls are always faster than wired calls
Because updateJobStatus returns no value at all
questions.explain: updateJobStatus performs DML, so it can't be marked cacheable=true, and it should only fire when a technician clicks the button -- exactly the case for an imperative call rather than @wire's automatic, reactive loading.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 15 to its definition in the current Named Credentials model.
right: One shared identity used for all users making a given callout
Holds the callout endpoint URL and references an External Credential for authentication
Each individual user supplies and stores their own separate credential
Holds the authentication protocol and secret-storage configuration for a callout
questions.explain: An External Credential holds the auth configuration; a Named Credential holds the endpoint and points at the External Credential; Named Principal shares one identity across users; Per-User gives each user their own stored credential.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 14, an Apex callout routed through a Named Credential uses an endpoint beginning with the literal prefix ________.
questions.explain: The endpoint starts with callout:<NamedCredentialName> rather than a literal URL, which is the required syntax for routing a callout through a Named Credential instead of hardcoding the URL and secret in Apex.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about this platform's callout error handling, per Lessons 14 and 15.
options: `http.send()` does not throw an Apex exception for a 4xx or 5xx HTTP status, so the code must check `getStatusCode()` explicitly
A transient failure (like a timeout) is retried, up to a capped number of attempts
A rejected failure (like an invalid serial number) is retried indefinitely until it succeeds
ManufacturerWarrantyTransientException and ManufacturerWarrantyRejectedException both extend a common ManufacturerWarrantyException class
Retry attempts have no limit, since the org's async Apex capacity is unlimited
questions.explain: The code must check the status code explicitly since callouts don't throw on HTTP error statuses; transient failures retry with a cap; and both custom exceptions extend a shared base. A rejected failure is deliberately NOT retried since it will fail identically again, and retries are capped specifically because async Apex capacity is finite and shared across the org.

questions.prompt: Dmitri wants one report showing Installation Jobs grouped by both Technician (rows) and Status (columns) at the same time. Per Lesson 16, which report format fits?
options: Tabular
Summary
Matrix
Joined
questions.explain: A Matrix report groups by rows and columns simultaneously, which is exactly what's needed to see Technician by Status in one view.

questions.prompt: Match each reporting/dashboard term from Lessons 16-17 to its definition.
right: A scheduled, automatic snapshot of a dashboard delivered to a user
Runs each component using the viewing user's own record access rather than a fixed running user
A report-only grouping of a field's values into named ranges, with no schema change
A report type exposing fields from an object plus specified related objects
questions.explain: A bucket field groups values without a new field; a custom report type adds related-object fields to a report; a dynamic dashboard runs per viewer; a subscription delivers a scheduled snapshot automatically.

questions.prompt: Match each documentation artifact from Lesson 21 to its purpose.
right: Records one design decision's status, context, decision, alternatives considered, and consequences
Shows how objects connect to each other
Describes, field by field, what each custom field means in plain language
questions.explain: The ERD shows connections between objects, the data dictionary explains individual fields in plain language, and an ADR documents one architecture decision with its alternatives and consequences.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 18, deploying with `sf project deploy start --test-level ________` runs every local Apex test as part of the deployment, enforcing the coverage requirement.
questions.explain: --test-level RunLocalTests runs all local Apex tests during the deployment itself, which is what actually enforces the 75% coverage requirement at deploy time.

questions.prompt: Select every item that is actually on Priya's code review checklist, per Lesson 19.
options: Is there a handler class, with the trigger body itself doing nothing but routing?
Are SOQL/DML statements kept outside of loops?
Does every pull request include at least 500 lines of new code?
Are callouts wrapped in try/catch with a specific exception type rather than a bare catch (Exception e)?
Is `with sharing` used unless there's a documented reason for `without sharing`?
questions.explain: Priya's checklist covers the handler pattern, loop-bound SOQL/DML, specific exception handling on callouts, and the with sharing default -- there is no line-count requirement on pull request size.

questions.prompt: Lesson 20 found that `WarrantyClaimTriggerHandler`'s original per-record query pattern passed Lesson 10's 50-record bulk test but would fail at 200 records in one transaction. Why?
options: Because 50 queries is within the 100-query synchronous limit, but 200 queries in one transaction exceeds that same limit, which the 50-record test never exercised
Because Apex cannot process more than 50 records in any transaction under any circumstances
Because the 50-record test used a different Asset for every claim
Because Lesson 10's test was written in a way that is syntactically invalid
questions.explain: One query per claim means 50 claims use 50 queries (safe, under the 100-query synchronous limit) while 200 claims in one transaction would use 200 queries, which exceeds that limit -- a failure mode the smaller test never triggered.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement from Lesson 20's performance review.
options: StaleInstallationJobBatch is already structurally safe at any volume because Batch Apex's chunking exists specifically for large record sets
TechnicianJobBoardController.getMyJobs filters on Technician__c, a lookup field that is indexed by default
The Case to Installation Job Flow's Get Records element is automatically exempt from any per-record query concerns because it's declarative
The fix for the claim coverage check is to query once for the whole batch into a Map, then look up each claim's contract inside the loop
Performance review only ever applies to Apex code, never to Flow
questions.explain: Batch Apex's chunking and the indexed Technician__c filter are both confirmed safe, and the Map-based refactor is the actual fix applied. The lesson explicitly argues the opposite of the last two options: a Flow's Get Records element can still run per record/interview and deserves the same bulk-load scrutiny as Apex, not an automatic pass because it's declarative.

questions.prompt: Put these seven Chapter 4 activities in the order this capstone performs them.
items: Build dashboards backed by those reports
Set up deployment via source-driven CI/CD
Apply testing and code review practices
questions.explain: Chapter 4 moves from reports to the dashboards that visualize them, into the deployment pipeline, then testing/code review, then a dedicated performance pass, then documentation of the decisions made along the way, and finally the retrospective that closes out the chapter by checking everything against the Definition of Done.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 23, why is a "narration-first, clicks-second" demo script more resilient than a rigid list of clicks?
options: It eliminates the need to ever use a scratch org for the demo
Each step's narration stays true and useful even if the live click fails, letting the presenter keep the story moving instead of stalling
It removes the need to prepare any script at all
It guarantees the live demo environment will never have a network issue
questions.explain: Writing narration that remains accurate regardless of whether the live action succeeds means a failed click doesn't stall the demo -- the presenter can still describe the result and continue the scenario.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 24, how should the question "Why Queueable and not Platform Events for the warranty submission?" be answered during the presentation?
options: By improvising a new justification on the spot, since no prior documentation addresses it
By citing the specific ADR from Lesson 21 that already documents Platform Events were considered and rejected as unnecessary complexity
By deflecting the question and moving to the next topic
By admitting the decision was arbitrary and had no real reasoning behind it
questions.explain: The ADR already documents this exact alternative and the reason it was rejected, which is the whole point of writing ADRs in Lesson 21 -- the presentation draws on evidence that already exists rather than improvising.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of feedback to the triage bucket it belongs in, per Lesson 25.
left: A genuine gap against the Definition of Done, discovered during the presentation
The Assign Technician subflow's simplified, non-certification-aware assignment logic
A suggestion to add an entirely new mobile app, unrelated to this capstone's scope
right: Out of scope
Fix before calling this done
Log as technical debt
questions.explain: A genuine Definition of Done gap must be fixed before calling the work done; the already-named, deliberate simplification is logged as technical debt; and a good idea unrelated to this capstone's actual scope is out of scope for this project.

questions.prompt: Select every item Lesson 25 lists as part of a "portfolio-ready" result for this capstone.
options: The Git repository, with real incremental commit history
The ERD and data dictionary
A paid Salesforce certification voucher
The five Architecture Decision Records
A recording of the demo
The retrospective
questions.explain: Portfolio-ready means the Git repository, the ERD and data dictionary, the five ADRs, a demo recording, and the retrospective -- together, not any single one alone. A certification voucher is never mentioned as part of this checklist.
